q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM( SELECT DISTINCT C.CUSTOMER_ID,COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY)= ( SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT ) ) TEMP
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM( SELECT DISTINCT C.CUSTOMER_ID,COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY)= ( SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT ) ) TEMP
counterexample: INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2), (3); INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 2);
explanation: Q1 groups customers by CUSTOMER_ID and checks if the count of distinct products they purchased is equal to the total count of distinct products in the PRODUCT table. Q2 first groups customers by CUSTOMER_ID and counts distinct products for each, then groups the results by CUSTOMER_ID again and checks if the count of distinct products is equal to the total count of distinct products in the PRODUCT table. The difference lies in the second GROUP BY in Q2, which causes it to return the same CUSTOMER_ID multiple times if they purchased the same number of distinct products as the total number of distinct products in the PRODUCT table.
counterexample_dsp: A customer who purchased all distinct products in the PRODUCT table, and another customer who purchased a different set of products that also matches the total number of distinct products in the PRODUCT table.
